stem: An adult client's oral temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). How should the nurse interpret this finding?

options.A: It is within the expected adult oral-temperature range and requires no illness assessment unless hypotension also develops.
options.B: It indicates hypothermia and should prompt warming measures before evaluating other possible causes.
options.C: It is only mildly elevated and below the usual fever range, so no additional assessment is needed unless it rises further.
options.D: It represents fever and warrants assessment of the client's symptoms and clinical context to identify a possible underlying cause.

rationale: MedlinePlus states that a high body temperature is fever and that an adult probably has a fever when oral temperature is above about 99°F to 99.5°F (37.2°C to 37.5°C), depending on time of day. It also notes that a temperature more than 1°F to 1.5°F above a person's normal temperature is fever and that fever can accompany many illnesses. An oral temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F) is therefore clearly febrile and should be interpreted with the client's symptoms and clinical context. A, B, and C misclassify the temperature or delay appropriate assessment.
educational_objective: Recognize a markedly elevated adult oral temperature as fever and assess associated symptoms and clinical context rather than treating the value as normal, hypothermic, or insignificant.
source_version_date: Temperature measurement reviewed January 14, 2026; current MedlinePlus fever guidance
source_locator: Temperature measurement — Normal Results and What Abnormal Results Mean; Fever — adult oral fever definition and Considerations.
source_claim_supported: High temperature is fever; adult oral temperatures well above normal, including 39.2°C, are febrile and should be interpreted in clinical context because fever may reflect infection or other illness.

source_original.stem: An adult client's oral temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). How should the nurse interpret this finding?

options.A: It is within the expected adult temperature range and requires no assessment for illness unless the client also develops hypotension.
options.B: It indicates hypothermia and should prompt warming measures before evaluating infectious, inflammatory, or other possible causes.
options.C: It is only a mildly elevated temperature below the usual fever threshold, so no additional assessment is needed unless it rises further.
options.D: It represents fever and warrants assessment for the underlying cause, associated symptoms, hydration, and other clinical findings.

source_original.rationale: An oral temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F) is clearly febrile. Option D is correct because the nurse should recognize fever and assess the surrounding clinical context and possible cause. Option A incorrectly places the value within the expected adult range. Option B reverses the interpretation by calling a high temperature hypothermia. Option C incorrectly describes 39.2°C as below the fever threshold and advises no additional assessment.
source_original.source_detail: NIH/NLM MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia — Temperature measurement: normal temperature varies; an oral temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F) is clearly febrile and should be interpreted in clinical context. correction_summary: Retained the key but removed unsupported universal requirements to assess hydration and named etiologic categories from the answer. Final wording stays with MedlinePlus-supported fever recognition plus symptom/clinical-context assessment.

audit_findings.exact_locator: Normal Results; What Abnormal Results Mean; Fever adult oral-temperature discussion.
audit_findings.claim_audit: 39.2°C is unambiguously above cited fever ranges; final answer does not invent an etiologic diagnosis or mandatory treatment.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrectly normalizes a clearly elevated temperature.
distractor_audit.D: Correct fever recognition with appropriate contextual assessment.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D accurately interprets the measurement.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are temperature interpretations; no second answer.
